extracted.intended_audience: researchers, journal editors, and readers interested in research integrity and peer review
extracted.subtask_short: detecting data fabrication in clinical trials
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and examples for identifying possible data fabrication in clinical trial and laboratory research, focusing on statistical screening of reported summary statistics, verification of primary data/instruments, and appropriate editorial responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statistical comparison of published distributions to expected distributions
rubrics_metrics.description: I extracted rates for categorical variables and means (SDs) for continuous variables, and compared these published distributions with distributions that would be expected by chance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect published summary statistics (categorical rates; means and SDs for continuous variables) and compare their distributions to theoretical/expected distributions under chance. This is a primary analytic approach used in the Carlisle analysis of 169 RCTs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use improbability (very small p-values) to flag likely fabrication
rubrics_metrics.description: The published distributions of 28/33 variables (85%) were inconsistent with the expected distributions, such that the likelihood of their occurring ranged from 1 in 25 to less than 1 in 10^33, equivalent to p values of 0.04 to < 1·10^33, respectively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat extremely small probabilities / tiny p-values for observed summary statistics as evidence warranting investigation. Example thresholds in the Carlisle example range from p≈0.04 down to p<<1e-30; many such improbabilities across variables strengthen suspicion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compare inconsistency rates against other authors as baseline
rubrics_metrics.description: Distributions for individual RCTs were inconsistent with the expected in 97/135 human studies by Fujii et al. ... compared with 12/139 RCTs by other authors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use comparison with contemporaneous/field peers as a baseline to judge whether an author's rate of implausible statistics is anomalous. A much higher proportion of inconsistent studies for one author than for others supports concern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examine both aggregate (across studies) and individual-RCT distribution inconsistencies
rubrics_metrics.description: In 142 human studies, 13/13 published continuous-variable distributions were inconsistent ... Distributions were inconsistent with the expected in 21/24 individual canine studies that reported more than two continuous variables.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Screen at two levels: pooled/aggregate across multiple studies and within individual trial reports (especially those reporting multiple continuous variables). High rates of inconsistency at either level are informative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verify existence of primary instruments and raw datasets (questionnaires, databases, patients)
rubrics_metrics.description: You could start by actually looking at the questionnaires. Do they exist at all? The implication is that the questionnaires, databases of answers, maybe even the patients(!) never existed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where possible, confirm that the questionnaires, databases, and other primary instruments exist and are preserved. Absence of primary instruments or datasets is a red flag for fabrication or nonexistence of subjects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Request original/raw data and primary files via the editor when in doubt
rubrics_metrics.description: If there is a doubt on reviewers' part, they can through Editor request say original image files, or raw mass spec data, or a pdb.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Peer reviewers or editors should request original/raw files (images, mass-spec raw data, structure files, machine-readable datasets) from authors when concerns arise. These may clarify or disprove suspected anomalies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize privacy constraints and use internal review to access identifiable patient files when necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: Usually study participants are granted anonymity. So you can’t just show patient files around as raw data. Only in the case of suspected fraud, you can hope for internal review, and for such purposes there usually is internal access to the patient files.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance confidentiality with investigatory needs: anonymized public raw data may not be possible; institutions' internal review processes can access patient-identifiable records to assess suspected fraud while preserving confidentiality externally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not overestimate the definitive power of raw data checks
rubrics_metrics.description: But the power of proof of so called raw data should not be overestimated anyway. If you want to forge a conclusion, you can always generate raw data under specific circumstances that you simply don’t report.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat raw data inspection as raising the hurdle for fraud but not as absolute proof. Fabricators can also fabricate raw spreadsheets; combine data checks with other evidence (metadata, provenance, independent corroboration).

rubrics_metrics.name: Be pragmatic about the form of requested primary data
rubrics_metrics.description: What are they going to ask for in this case? Bankers boxes full of questionnaires? At best all they can get in this case is some kinda excel file…
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Request feasible, machine-readable versions of primary data (e.g., spreadsheets, exported databases) rather than impractical paper archives. Practical access improves the chance of meaningful review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate ethical approval concerns from data reliability
rubrics_metrics.description: The statement, which cites lack of ethics approval for some studies, is mute on the issue of whether Fujii’s results were, in fact, reliable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Absence of IRB/ethics approval is a serious procedural violation and justification for investigation, but it does not by itself establish that reported results were fabricated; investigations should explicitly address both ethical approval and data reliability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use editorial actions (statement of concern, investigation, and retraction) when fabrication is suspected
rubrics_metrics.description: He said he has grave concerns about the possibility of manipulation or fabrication in Dr. Fujii’s published research. This will be investigated, and compromised papers in Anesthesia & Analgesia will be retracted. The journal has issued a statement of concern about the papers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When statistical or other evidence suggests fabrication, journals should (a) investigate promptly, (b) issue a statement of concern if appropriate, and (c) retract compromised papers once evidence supports that step.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider prior expressions of concern and historical criticisms
rubrics_metrics.description: As we reported yesterday, a 2000 letter expressing incredulity about the validity of his results — said he has grave concerns ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Review the publication and correspondence history (letters, prior critiques) for earlier doubts about an author's work; repeated past concerns strengthen the case for closer scrutiny.
